\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}

\title{Efficiency Loss in Repeated Congestion Games with Boundedly Rational Agents}
\author{A.~Petrov and L.~Nakamura}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
Congestion games are everywhere in modern infrastructure, from traffic
networks to cloud computing markets. In these games, selfish agents choose
resources, and the cost of each resource depends on how many agents use
it. A classical result tells us that the price of anarchy of atomic
congestion games is bounded by a small constant. However, most of this
literature assumes that agents are perfectly rational and that the game is
played only once.

In reality, neither assumption holds. Commuters learn routes over weeks of
repeated interaction, and their decisions are shaped by habit, imperfect
information, and bounded memory. Understanding what happens in this regime
matters: if the efficiency loss under bounded rationality is much larger
than the classical bounds suggest, then mechanism design based on one-shot
equilibrium analysis may be badly misguided.

In this paper we study repeated atomic congestion games in which agents
follow a no-regret learning dynamic with finite memory. We show that the
average efficiency loss converges to a quantity that depends smoothly on
the memory length, and we identify a threshold phenomenon: below a
critical memory length, the loss grows linearly with the number of agents,
while above it the loss remains bounded by a constant. Our results suggest
that modest improvements in traveler information systems can have
outsized effects on aggregate congestion.

\end{document}
